Higher demand for terraced homes as some buyers priced out of semi-detached segment: Huttons
article:
Semi-detached homes saw the biggest price jump among landed housing segments in the last quarter, despite lower volume.

Excluding Good Class Bungalows (GCBs) and strata landed homes, the prices of landed houses grew by 3.7% q-o-q in 3Q2026 to an average of $2,275 psf, URA data compiled by Huttons Data Analytics showed.

Overall volume and average price of landed homes

While all landed home segments saw price increases, the semi-detached segment recorded the biggest growth, rising 4.7% from an average of $1,989 psf in 2Q2026 to $2,082 psf in the last quarter.

Prices of terraced homes rose 2.7% q-o-q to $2,400 psf across the same period, while those for detached homes grew 1.4% to $2,046 psf.

This comes despite fewer semi-detached homes transacted. The segment saw 143 units sold in 3Q2026, falling 13.3% q-o-q. In contrast, terraced home sales remained steady in the last quarter — at 300 units, on a par with the 301 sold in 2Q2026.

Detached homes saw a slight decrease in sales volume, going from 50 units in 2Q2026 to 44 units in the last quarter.

“As some buyers were priced out of the semi-detached market, demand shifted towards terraced homes,” Huttons stated in its latest quarterly report on the landed market, published on Oct 26.

Transaction volume and average prices of landed homes by segment

In absolute terms, semi-detached homes were transacted at an average of $6.9 million in 3Q2026, rising 4.2% q-o-q. In comparison, prices of terraced and detached homes declined by 1.9% and 4.9% to $4.7 million and $13.0 million, respectively.

Overall, a total of 487 landed housing transactions were recorded in 3Q2023, excluding GCBs and strata landed homes. This is 5.6% less than the 516 deals logged in the previous quarter.

Huttons attributed the fall to seasonal factors that included the Lunar Seventh Month, along with slower activity in the HDB and private condo resale markets.

It added that rising land costs were prompting more buyers to opt for smaller landed properties. “The average land size of transacted landed homes shrank from 3,079 sq ft in 2Q2026 to 2,910 sq ft in 3Q2026,” the report stated.

In addition to smaller plots, landed homebuyers were also turning to shorter tenures, noted Lee Sze Teck, Huttons’ senior director of data analytics.

This comes amid a broadening price gap between freehold and 999-year leasehold homes compared to those with 99-year tenures.

“The price gap between 999-year leasehold/freehold and 99-year leasehold landed homes in 3Q2026 widened to 51.2%, the biggest since 2020,” he said.

As a result, there was a slightly higher proportion of 99-year leasehold landed transactions in the last quarter. These homes accounted for 15.6% of all landed housing deals in 3Q2026, up by 2.4 percentage points and the highest since 1Q2025.

Looking ahead, landed property volumes may “dip slightly” in 4Q2026 due to the year-end holidays, Lee noted. Nonetheless, backed by persistent demand, their prices should “stay firm”.

title: URA awards Marina Gardens Lane GLS site to EL Development at $1,243 psf ppr
article:
URA has awarded the tender for a Government Land Sale (GLS) site at Marina Gardens Lane to EL Development for $450.1 million, or $1,243 psf per plot ratio (psf ppr).

The tender for the residential site with ground-floor commercial space closed on Oct 15, with EL Development the sole bidder.

The developer’s offer fell below analysts' expectations of three to six bids and a top bid between $1,350 and $1,650 psf ppr.

The land rate is 11.3% lower than the $1,402 psf ppr Kingsford Group paid in 2023 for a neighbouring plot, which is now the 937-unit One Marina Gardens .

However, it is higher than the $984 psf ppr offer URA rejected in 2024 for a nearby GLS site at Marina Gardens Crescent. The sole bid by GuocoLand, Hong Leong Holdings and TID for the white site was deemed to be too low.

The Marina Gardens Lane plot awarded to EL Development measures 64,659 sq ft and has a maximum gross floor area of 362,119 sq ft. The 99-year leasehold site can yield about 390 homes and up to 1,615 sq ft of first-floor commercial space.

Based on the $1,243 psf ppr land rate, analysts predict future homes on the site could launch at average prices ranging from $2,500 to around $2,900 psf.

title: Shangri-La Singapore unveils refurbished Valley Wing with two Presidential Suites
article:
Shangri-La Singapore has unveiled its refurbished Valley Wing, with redesigned guest rooms and suites, including two Presidential Suites.

The luxury hotel’s refurbishment covered the Valley Wing's Executive Rooms, Executive Suites, Premier Suites and two Presidential Suites: the Shangri-La Suite and Singapore Suite.

Located within Shangri-La Singapore's 15-acre (6.07ha) grounds along Orange Grove Road, near Orchard Road, the Valley Wing has its own private driveway, lobby and check-in area, separate from the hotel's other accommodation wings.

Interiors inspired by Singapore's heritage

The redesigned interiors draw inspiration from Singapore's historic shophouses and tropical landscape, combining Asian decorative elements with European classical influences.

Geometric latticework, architectural mouldings and decorative panels reference traditional shophouse architecture.

Botanical wallpaper depicting tropical foliage, flowering branches and wildlife complements the soft greens, muted golds and warm neutrals used throughout the rooms and suites.

The Executive Rooms feature updated furnishings and seating areas, while the larger Executive and Premier Suites provide additional living space.

Two refurbished Presidential Suites

The largest accommodation in the hotel is the 348 sq m (3,746 sq ft) Shangri-La Suite, which has separate living and dining areas for private gatherings and entertaining.

The suite includes an upgraded 85-inch television, a private gym, its own lift and dedicated 24-hour butler service.

The second Presidential Suite, named the Singapore Suite, has two bedrooms, spacious living areas, panoramic views and a private whirlpool bath.

Both suites feature wall murals depicting tropical landscapes and floral designs, as well as upholstered furnishings and warm-toned interiors.

Exclusive facilities for Valley Wing guests

The Valley Wing retains its dedicated guest facilities, including the Summit Room, where breakfast is served, and the Valley Wing Lounge.

Guests can enjoy afternoon tea, champagne and refreshments at the lounge throughout the day, followed by evening cocktails and canapés.

“With this transformation, our vision was to honour the timeless elegance and sense of exclusivity that guests have come to cherish, while introducing a renewed expression of luxury that feels both contemporary and deeply connected to Singapore's heritage,” says Stephan Kapek, vice-president of operations and general manager of Shangri-La Singapore.

title: European gas hits €97 for first time since 2022 on winter risks
article:
(Oct 26): European natural gas topped €97 a megawatt-hour for the first time since 2022 as concerns mount about the region’s fragile supply balance this winter and the outlook for the Middle East conflict.

Benchmark futures extended last week’s advance by as much as 3.5% early Monday. Traders expect an uptick in heating demand in the coming days, with temperatures set to drop across the continent. That would coincide with tight global gas supplies and set the stage for bidding wars with other buyers, such as Asia.

Expectations are fading that the market could ease any time soon amid continued hostilities and supply disruptions in the Persian Gulf. Iran is bracing for a fresh US bombing campaign around America’s November midterms and is preparing to retaliate across the Middle East, Bloomberg News reported.

Volatile liquefied natural gas flows have played a crucial role in supplying Europe’s energy since the 2022 crisis, leaving it vulnerable to potential disruptions as the continent enters its peak-demand season with abnormally low fuel inventories. EU gas-storage sites are about 75% full, the lowest for the season in records going back to 2009, while those in Germany are at just over 61%.

European gas prices are still well below the peaks of the last energy crisis but the latest advance risks fanning inflation and weighing on economic activity. So far in October, Europe’s LNG imports have lagged last year’s levels despite typically jumping this time of year.

See also: Oil declines from six-month high as traders assess Mideast risks

Dutch front-month futures, Europe’s gas benchmark, traded 3.2% higher at €96.88 a megawatt-hour by 8.50am in Amsterdam. As a result of the rising gas prices, French month-ahead power futures exceeded €200 a megawatt-hour for the first time since January 2023.

title: Palantir’s fast-selling US$170 windbreaker shows its Korea appeal
article:
(Oct 26): Palantir Technologies Inc has spent years selling governments and companies its data analytics. In South Korea, it’s also selling US$170 ($217) windbreakers — and they are flying off the shelves.

Thousands of fans descended on a two-storey pop-up store in Seoul last week to snap up hoodies, T-shirts and hats bearing Palantir’s logo, with a Korea-exclusive windbreaker selling out within hours.

The frenzy underscores an unusual level of enthusiasm for a company better known elsewhere as a secretive military and surveillance contractor that has faced protests over its work with the US military and immigration authorities.

Palantir has increasingly sought to cultivate that fandom. It has released everything from tennis whites to a US$239 French chore coat, using merchandise to build a more approachable public identity around a company whose core products most consumers will never encounter.

“We take the merchandise very seriously,” said Eliano Younes, Palantir’s head of engagement. “For a lot of these folks, the only time they’ll ever really get to touch Palantir is through the merchandise.”

That strategy has found greater success in South Korea where the government and some of its biggest industrial companies are pouring money into artificial intelligence. Sales from last week’s event jumped 30% from 2025, while the country has at times ranked as Palantir’s second-largest market after the US for online merchandise, according to Younes.

See also: Musk claims US$40 bil chips debt closed, yet talks ongoing

That enthusiasm matters because Korea is emerging as one of Palantir’s promising avenues for overseas growth. chief executive officer Alex Karp last year called the country the “second most interesting market” after the US.

The fandom also offers Palantir a way to cultivate a broader and more approachable public identity as it expands globally. The company has faced criticism over its handling of data and its ties to the Donald Trump administration.

But in Seoul, the company is making gradual inroads.

See also: OpenAI resumes training AI — without internet access

Since opening its South Korean office in 2022, Palantir has been expanding its presence. Last week, it signed a deal with Posco Future M to accelerate its AI-driven transformation. It also struck partnerships with Korean telecommunications giant KT in March 2025 and defence firm LIG Nex1 in March.

Dan Do, who works in the dental industry, has been a Palantir investor since it went public in 2020. Drawn initially to the company’s “defend the West” narrative and government business, he later saw potential in its Foundry commercial software. His frequent posts about Palantir on X earned him early access to the Seoul event, which he flew from Sydney to attend.

“The company puts a lot of effort into building community,” said Do, clutching an armload of streetwear to buy.

In Korea, public and corporate enthusiasm for AI is high. Seoul’s trend-driven consumer culture also gives Palantir an opportunity to present itself not simply as a defence contractor but as a technology brand with a devoted following, said Yoon Young-bin of OAAH Agency, an experience-curation service.

The country is home to globally important semiconductor, shipbuilding, automotive and manufacturing companies — all potential partners for Palantir, which is seeking to embed its AI and data software. The government is also accelerating spending on artificial intelligence, tripling its AI budget this year to 10.1 trillion won (US$7.6 billion or $9.8 billion) as it embraces the concept of sovereign AI.

The latest merchandise to drop was a Korea-exclusive white nylon windbreaker that would “look really nice on the golf course”, said Younes, adding that the sport’s popularity in Korea factored into its development.

The inaugural Seoul pop-up last year attracted more than 5,000 fans over two days. The response prompted Palantir to increase inventory this time, impose limits on how many items each visitor can buy and introduce pre-registration. Even so, some products quickly sold out.

Brand strategists say merchandise can turn consumers into walking billboards, increasing exposure both in real life and online as people share photos of swag on social media. Flashing an emblem can also foster a shared identity, helping brands form and expand fandoms, said Kim Yong-seok, the CEO of Talksulting, a brand-strategy firm.

In Palantir’s case, “the main consumers are likely to be individuals who find the potential of Palantir’s technology to resonate, investors who have high hopes for the company’s future and fans who have developed an affinity for the brand itself”, Kim added.

title: Chinese carmakers overtake Japan in Europe for first time
article:
(Oct 26): Chinese automakers outsold Japanese rivals in Europe for the first time over a full quarter, underscoring how quickly brands like BYD Co and Chery Automobile Co are gaining ground in the region.

Registrations of Chinese-branded cars roughly doubled from a year earlier in September to make up 12.7% of total sales across the region, led by hybrids, according to market researcher Dataforce. That’s put them ahead of Japanese manufacturers including Toyota Motor Corp at 11.9%.

While European manufacturers like Volkswagen AG or Renault SA still dominate the region, the speed of China’s surge has been a surprise. Five years ago, Chinese brands accounted for barely 1% of European sales. Japan’s automakers, by contrast, have spent decades building their position in Europe.

Toyota has sold cars in the region since 1963 and now operates factories across the continent, while Nissan Motor Co has produced vehicles at its Sunderland plant in the UK since 1986. China’s offering is especially successful in the UK, where Chery’s Jaecoo 7 SUV was the country’s best-selling model in March and September.

The shift is a double whammy for Europe’s struggling manufacturers. China’s drivers are deserting VW and BMW AG in their biggest market in favour of domestic rivals, who are churning out new models faster and at lower cost. And shrinking demand in China is forcing BYD and others to look for new markets.

Earlier this month, Chery, BYD and Geely’s Zeekr showed off a range of new models at the Paris car show, offering well-priced cars like the BYD Dolphin G DM-i, a compact plug-in hybrid specifically developed for Europe. Bringing their EV lineups to Europe also positions them to benefit from a jump in demand as fuel prices hit record highs.

The European Union is trying to temper an expansion that is partly fuelled by state-backed subsidies. After adding extra tariffs on China-made battery-electric vehicles, the bloc this month agreed in principle to curb fast-growing imports of hybrid cars from China.

See also: Nextdc CEO to forgo bonus after Australia data centre delay

Amid speculation of future measures, shipments of hybrids have accelerated.

Separately, the EU is considering new rules that would favor locally made cars when granting subsidies and other incentives. The proposals include linking some company-car tax benefits to European production, a powerful tool in many countries like Germany where corporate and fleet buyers dominate.

Carmakers like Mercedes-Benz Group AG have welcomed the political backing, but warned of distortions to global supply chains, driving costs up. Countries including the UK, Türkiye and Morocco ship vehicles and parts to the EU that could struggle because of Made in Europe rules.

Chinese manufacturers have been preparing to produce locally already. Chery is preparing production in Barcelona and BYD is nearing the completion of a manufacturing site in Hungary. Zhejiang Leapmotor Technology Co has started making its B10 SUV at Stellantis NV’s plant in Zaragoza, Spain, as part of the companies’ joint venture.

title: Food-delivery firm Meituan aims to raise US$1 bil in bond sale
article:
(Oct 26): Chinese food-delivery giant Meituan is seeking to raise the equivalent of about US$1 billion through its offshore yuan bond offering, according to people familiar with the matter, as it joins a growing wave of issuers tapping the dim sum debt market.

The company has obtained approval from Chinese regulators to raise a larger amount offshore but decided to preserve part of the quota for dollar bond refinancing when market conditions are favourable. Meituan representatives told investors during a call on Monday, the people said, asking not to be identified discussing private matters. The quota is set to expire next September, they added.

The dim sum bond offering is expected to be priced on Tuesday, the people said.

Meituan is raising the debt as competition has eased in China’s food delivery and retail business following a crackdown by authorities, taking some pressure off the sector’s big players. The firm reported a surprise quarterly profit in August and has also slowed its overseas expansion.

Proceeds from the sale, which is the company’s second-ever dim sum bond offering, will be used mainly to refinance offshore yuan-denominated loans, the people said.

Meituan raised about US$3 billion from a sale of dollar securities and offshore yuan notes last year in its largest regular bond issuance ever. It expects capital expenditure to reach around RMB20 billion in 2026 and increase modestly in 2027, according to the people.

See also: Chinese copper titan He Jinbi jailed for life over Maike fraud

Yuan financing has become increasingly appealing to both Chinese and foreign firms for its lower costs. Government and corporate issuers have sold over RMB1 trillion of dim sum notes outside mainland China this year, an all-time high, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. Earlier this month, Tencent Holdings Ltd raised RMB26 billion of such notes, surpassing its dollar tranche in a single offering for the first time.

Like its Chinese tech peers, Meituan has developed its own large language models for artificial intelligence, called the LongCat series. But the company isn’t updating its AI offerings as fast as rivals such as Alibaba Group Holding Ltd or ByteDance Ltd.

title: Bitcoin dips below US$80,000 as AI-related market selloff deepens
article:
(Oct 26): Bitcoin retreated below US$80,000 on Monday as broader risk-off sentiment ahead of a Federal Reserve meeting and concerns over the artificial intelligence trade weighed on cryptocurrencies.

The largest digital asset fell as much as 1.4% to under US$79,300 before paring some losses to trade around US$80,000 in afternoon trading in Asia. Smaller tokens including Ether, XRP and Solana also declined. The moves came after investors pulled US$772.4 million from US-listed spot bitcoin exchange-traded funds on Thursday and Friday, a sharp reversal from more than US$1 billion of net inflows earlier in the week.

The declines accompanied a broader market slump that extended from last week as investors questioned massive spending on AI and looked toward this week’s earnings reports from tech giants for clues about the outlook. The Kospi Index in South Korea — a bellwether for the AI trade — fell 0.2% and chip-related stocks were among the biggest decliners in Japan’s Nikkei.

“Bitcoin has so far been relatively resilient to the AI debt concerns that are weighing on all risk assets,” said Caroline Mauron, co-founder of Orbit Markets. “The market focus is now on the Fed meeting, followed by the US midterm elections.”

Bitcoin remains in the risk-off basket for many systematic funds and algorithmic traders, leaving it vulnerable to deteriorating sentiment, said Pratik Kala, portfolio manager at Apollo Crypto.

See also: Bitcoin falls below US$83,000 as AI jitters weigh on sentiment

Kala pointed to online discussions about AI, including comments from SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk about potential consolidation next year, as contributing to market strain. Advances in AI have also exacerbated potential security risks for crypto, making some investors skittish, he added.

title: Chinese PCB maker Dongshan raises US$1.3 bil in HK listing
article:
(Oct 26): Suzhou Dongshan Precision Manufacturing Co, a printed circuit board maker, raised about HK$9.9 billion in Hong Kong’s biggest listing in nearly two months, which hit a volatile market for companies related to the artificial intelligence build out.

The company priced about 113.8 million shares at HK$86.80 apiece, compared to a maximum of HK$93.80, according to a filing to the city’s stock exchange on Sunday, which confirmed an earlier Bloomberg News report. Dongshan said it had not exercised an upsize option. Trading is expected to begin on Oct 28. The price represents a discount of about 35% to the Friday close of its Shenzhen-listed stock, which is up 35% this year even after a nearly 60% slide from a June peak.

Dongshan, which makes the components that are the intricate electronic backbone of AI servers, is braving the market at a tricky time across Asia, especially for companies in its business.

First-time listings have raised more than US$50 billion in Hong Kong this year, edging closer to the US$57.8 billion record set in 2010 but rising bond yields and poor deal performance are making investors and issuers more cautious. A string of withdrawals and delays, including by major data centre operators in the region, has prompted some companies to put near-term listing plans on hold.

“With Dongshan’s Shenzhen share price declining substantially, the reference valuation for its Hong Kong offering has also fallen,” said Francis Tan, Asia chief strategist at Indosuez Wealth Management in Singapore. “Investors still want exposure to the AI revolution but they are increasingly demanding earnings visibility rather than simply buying the narrative.”

See also: Hong Kong IPO red flags include sudden loans and secret handshakes

The company’s Shenzhen-listed shares dropped as much as 5.6% in early Monday trading.

Chinese technology stocks have been particularly hit hard, with no end in sight for a deepening selloff as investors confront the realities of an economy that’s weak enough to erode corporate profits but not to trigger forceful new stimulus.

The world’s second-largest equities market has lost US$3.5 trillion in value from a peak in May, data compiled by Bloomberg show. The rout intensified last week, pushing the onshore benchmark CSI 300 Index into a bear market and a technology sector gauge in Hong Kong toward erasing all its gains since Beijing’s sweeping growth support package two years ago.

Dongshan Precision’s listing leaned heavily on cornerstone investors, which get guaranteed allocation in the deal in exchange for holding the stock for at least six months. They include JPMorgan Asset Management, Alibaba Group Holding Ltd, CPE and Montage Technology Co, who agreed to buy a combined 50% of the offering. Jane Street Group and Jump Trading LLC are also among them.

The Suzhou-based company makes PCBs and optical transceivers, key components for AI. It’s the third-largest PCB supplier in an US$85.2 billion global market, according to its prospectus.

UBS Group AG, Guotai Haitong Securities Co, GF Securities Co and Citic Securities Co are joint sponsors for the Hong Kong listing.

title: Jio’s record India IPO falls short of record payday for bankers
article:
(Oct 26): Jio Platforms Ltd raised a record amount of funds for billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s digital and telecommunications giant but it proved to be far less lucrative for the bankers handling the deal.

The company is paying about 1.96 billion rupees in fees to the 19 banks on the roughly US$3.1 billion IPO, according to filings. That amounts to about 0.65% of the issue size, trailing the fee pools of several previous offerings in India.

Fierce competition among investment bankers in India has compressed fees, particularly for marquee deals. Firms are often willing to accept thinner economics for a coveted role in high-profile transactions. The payoff can instead come through league-table rankings, bragging rights and credentials that help win the next big pitch.

That is a far cry from the days when Hyundai Motor India Ltd paid about 4.9 billion rupees to bankers for its then-record 278 billion-rupee IPO in 2024. Paytm parent One 97 Communications Ltd paid about 3.2 billion rupees for its 183 billion-rupee offering in 2021 while Swiggy Ltd handed out about 2.8 billion rupees for its 113 billion-rupee share sale.

Those types of windfalls have been elusive of late. National Stock Exchange of India Ltd, another blockbuster IPO this year, paid about 1.9 billion rupees to a syndicate of 20 banks that worked on its roughly US$2.4 billion offering, equivalent to about 0.8% of the issue size. Bankers split fees of just 46.3 million rupees for SBI Funds Management of India Ltd’s billion-dollar offering in July.

See also: JSW Steel’s 2Q profit more than triples on higher prices

Investor enthusiasm, meanwhile, has been anything but restrained. Jio’s IPO was fully subscribed within the first 100 minutes of bidding and had attracted bids for nearly 22 times the shares on offer by Friday, according to BSE Ltd data.

title: Musk claims US$40 bil chips debt closed, yet talks ongoing
article:
(Oct 26): Elon Musk said SpaceX has closed a US$40 billion ($51 billion) debt deal to pay for the chips it needs to fuel its artificial intelligence (AI) ambitions. People familiar with the discussions, though, told Bloomberg News that talks over pricing were still ongoing.

“SpaceX closed $40B of debt for GPUs,” Musk wrote in a post on X, referring to Nvidia Corp’s graphics processing units. He went on to suggest that debt markets had all but shut for neoclouds depending solely on revenue streams from AI data centres. “That means the 200+ neoclouds are going to see guppy-level death and consolidation,” Musk wrote. “Some will make it through, but not many.”

Musk’s comments came on the heels of a tumultuous week for the AI industry in debt markets as concern mounted over the rapid spending, and limited profits so far to show for it. With investors demanding increasingly large premiums to finance the AI buildout, the volatility roiled pricing discussions over the SpaceX debt, which is being structured as private bonds to be issued by an off-balance sheet entity.

As of late Sunday in New York, those conversations remained ongoing and the deal hadn’t priced, people with knowledge of the discussions said. The parties are still working on finalising the debt package in the coming days, they said.

More broadly in markets recently, much of the investor angst has been focused on the so-called neoclouds, which sell high-end computing power to technology companies. Noting SpaceX’s revenue from its Starlink business and rocket launches, Musk sought to differentiate his company from those businesses.

“As of the past few weeks, debt markets have almost entirely shut off access to money for any company that doesn’t have substantial revenue independent of AI data centres,” Musk said in his post. He later said that SpaceX won’t buy any neoclouds, calling it “pointless”.

See also: OpenAI resumes training AI — without internet access

SpaceX, which is rated investment-grade by the three largest credit graders, has seen the price of its own debt tumble in recent weeks. Credit-default swaps tied to SpaceX, which are used to insure against losses on the company’s debt, surged last week to a record 266 basis points at the close of trading Friday, a level more typical of a junk-rated borrower.

Bankers led by Goldman Sachs Group Inc have been discussing the chips debt structure with investors led by Apollo Global Management Inc, with Apollo-backed Atlas SP slated to manage the entity, people familiar with the matter said last week, asking not to be identified discussing private information. Pacific Investment Management Co has also considered investing, according to the people. The debt was expected to be issued in the form of private placements called 144a, the people said.

With the latest structure, SpaceX would avoid a repeat of a financing attempt last year by Musk’s AI startup, xAI. In that deal, an entity sought as much as US$20 billion of off-balance sheet debt through a sale-leaseback agreement with Valor Equity Partners. But SpaceX ultimately had to record about US$13 billion of that debt after it was declared a “failed sale-leaseback arrangement”, according to SpaceX’s latest earnings report.

The debt raise comes after strong third quarter earnings, with SpaceX’s AI unit turning a profit for the first time. The enterprise is increasingly driving revenue by selling computing power from its Memphis data centres to external AI labs and hyperscalers.

During SpaceX’s earnings call, chief financial officer Bret Johnsen indicated that the company was in discussions with lenders over further borrowing.

“We have a lot of conviction that we are going to be able to do this in a very measured fashion and continue to keep ourselves in that IG status along the way,” he said, pointing at the firm’s investment-grade rating.

title: Chinese copper titan He Jinbi jailed for life over Maike fraud
article:
(Oct 26): He Jinbi, one of the biggest names in Chinese copper trading, has been sentenced to life in prison over fraud and other offences committed by the company he founded, Maike Metals International Co.

A court in the western Chinese city of Xi’an found Maike guilty of contract fraud, bribery and other offences last month, and handed its 61-year-old boss, He, a life sentence, according to people familiar with the verdict. The ruling found Maike’s conduct had exposed several Chinese banks to more than US$1 billion of potential losses, the people added, asking not to be named due to the sensitivity of the issue.

He — whose company was forced into restructuring in 2023 after a liquidity crisis stemming from Covid-19-era disruptions — has appealed the verdict. Members of the family, the defence team and He himself did not respond to Bloomberg telephone calls and voice messages.

The judgment has not been made public. While China does have online databases for most legal proceedings, political and other exceptions for sensitive cases can allow courts to hold back publication.

He Jinbi’s defence, argued during proceedings that neither the company nor its founder intended to commit fraud. Maike worked with banks for more than a decade and regularly repaid its loans, striving to do so even when upheaval due to pandemic restrictions reduced cash flows. At least some losses at the lenders stemmed instead from inadequate internal risk controls and procedures, they said.

A personable, charismatic figure, He was part of a group of enterprising traders who made fortunes during the rush for commodities in the early 2000s, as China began to urbanise and develop at a breakneck pace. Maike, which he had founded with friends in Xi’an in 1993 with a RMB50,000 loan (close to US$8,700 at the time), shifted from mechanical and electrical products to focus on scrap metal, copper wire and refined copper.

See also: Food-delivery firm Meituan aims to raise US$1 bil in bond sale

Maike built a position as a key link between international miners, traders and buyers. At its peak, the group handled one in every four tonnes of copper imported into the world’s top consumer of the metal.

The company placed bold bets, becoming a pioneer in the practice of borrowing against the massive volumes of metal He was shipping and storing in warehouses. Maike was also at the forefront of a trend that saw many Chinese conglomerates expand into the booming real estate sector, investing in the hotels and business centres.

In 2022 the company’s finances came under pressure as Covid-19 restrictions upended business and a downturn in China’s property market hurt its investments. A sharp fall in copper prices added to the strain. He acknowledged that year that Maike had sought help to address a liquidity crisis.

See also: Sinking profits turn China’s US$3.5 tril stock rout into trap

As Maike struggled to meet its obligations, creditors began taking action. In October 2023, Maike executives reported losing touch with He, and believed he had been detained by police. Maike filed for bankruptcy the following month.

Xiamen Xindeco Ltd, a state-owned company and one of Maike’s major creditors, won a bid to lead the restructuring of Maike and 25 affiliated companies, according to an exchange filing last December.

Xindeco said it would invest RMB285 million in cash. Under the plan, one of its units would take a 75% stake in a newly formed company consolidating Maike’s remaining trading and logistics assets, including facilities in Shanghai’s free-trade zone and offices in Shanghai, Xi’an and Shenzhen. A bankruptcy service trust in Shaanxi province will hold the remaining 25%, the company said in December.

title: BYD’s Korea expansion challenges Hyundai dominance on home turf
article:
(Oct 26): When Lee Seongdong decided to replace his 2016 Chevrolet Spark in April, a two-year wait for Hyundai Motor Co’s Casper Electric was already pushing him toward BYD Co’s Dolphin. He was so impressed by the feature-rich ride that he signed a contract on the spot.

The price was attractive too: the Dolphin hatchback starts at 24.5 million won (US$18,500 or $24,000), though discounts meant Lee paid less than 23 million won — similar to a subsidised Casper Electric, which can be bought at about 22 million won in Seoul, but only in its bare-bones trim. Combined with not having to wait for longer than South Korea’s mandatory military service to take delivery, the 47-year-old YouTuber said the BYD was “way too good to pass up”.

Lee’s purchase is part of a burgeoning shift underway as BYD brings its low-cost strategy, which is already winning it market share in Europe, to increasingly price-sensitive buyers in South Korea. Bloomberg Intelligence’s data shows a ninefold jump in BYD’s EV and hybrid sales from January to August to almost 18,000 units, as Hyundai’s comparable sales fell 6% to about 139,000.

The momentum extended into September, when BYD’s registrations hit 20,000 — double its initial goal for the year, according to Korea Automobile & Mobility Association data.

BYD’s rapid ascent means it’s overtaken Volvo and Toyota Motor Corp in the ranks of foreign carmakers in Korea — a significant milestone given it only entered the passenger car market in early 2025 and, in July, lost access to government subsidies after not meeting some requirements. That’s a growing risk to local heavyweights Hyundai Motor Co and Kia Corp, which despite still holding a combined 72% share of the domestic market, are struggling to compete with the lower-priced, technology-focused models on offer by BYD.

See also: Chinese market is gone for Western automakers, says Volvo CEO

For the first time since 2010 — excluding the 2020 pandemic slump — Hyundai’s annual global sales will likely fall below four million units, missing its 4.16 million target, according to Samsung Securities Co analyst Esther Yim.

“The biggest driver of their slowdown is Chinese competition,” Yim wrote in a recent note. “Chinese EV makers’ aggressive export push has ignited intense price wars everywhere except the US and India, and Hyundai and Kia are underperforming in all those markets.”

Chinese automakers are accelerating their push into Korea. BYD is broadening its lineup with the Sealion 6 DM-i plug-in hybrid at 37.5 million won, the cheapest in its segment. Geely Automobile Holdings Ltd’s premium brand Zeekr began deliveries of its 7X electric SUV last week after surpassing 1,500 preorders, while XPeng Inc and Chery Automobile Co have set up local entities ahead of their market debuts.

See also: Porsche locks-in on the super-sportscar segment with the Mission S

Speaking at an event this month, Lee Jae-kyu, a senior vice-president overseeing vehicle development at Hyundai Motor Group, said he felt “despair” at the design and pricing edge Chinese automakers displayed at the recent Paris Motor Show.

“While European carmakers presented uninspiring designs and technology, Chinese vehicles offered superior design at prices roughly US$10,000 cheaper,” Lee said. “I couldn’t shake the thought that European companies will go under soon, and even our group is structured in a way that it could eventually be swallowed by China.”

Despite BYD’s rapid gains, analysts say Chinese brands face long-term hurdles due to sparse service infrastructure, high repair costs, steep insurance premiums and swift depreciation. In online driver communities, BYD owners regularly complain about spare parts delays and high repair bills, with minor bumper and fender benders exceeding 11 million won in some cases.

BYD plans to expand its South Korea service locations to 26 from 20 by the end of this year. The Shenzhen-based company’s low-price strategy will ultimately be tested against Hyundai and Kia’s network of more than 1,200 domestic service centres, according to Brian Lee at CLSA Securities Korea Ltd.

“Right now, everyone is focused purely on the sticker price,” he said. “But as the market matures and resale value, service access and maintenance costs become clear, their overall appeal could fade.”

Still, expansion in new foreign markets is critical for Chinese automakers as they face slowing demand at home, growing barriers in Europe, and are effectively shut out of the US. In contrast, Korea imposes an import tariff of just 8% on Chinese passenger cars and in August excluded EVs from a bill granting tax credits to domestic manufacturers, leaving Hyundai and Kia with few policy shields against cheap Chinese imports.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

Last month, KAMA — representing South Korea’s five automakers also including GM Korea, Renault Korea and KG Mobility — urged parliament to pass tax incentives and policy support.

“The penetration of Chinese EVs could trigger the collapse of not just domestic EV makers, but the entire auto industry,” the group warned in a statement.

Growing concerns over China’s rapid push have prompted South Korean lawmakers to introduce a bipartisan bill this month proposing tax credits covering up to 50% of annual domestic production costs for strategic industries, including EVs.

For buyers like Lee, the Dolphin owner, the broader policy worries mirror what he sees in the market: Chinese brands are raising the competitive bar.

“I hope our domestic auto industry succeeds, but in the end, you have to win through open market competition,” Lee said. “Everyone needs to stay alert and compete.”

title: Sembcorp explores supplying low-carbon power to Singtel’s Nxera
article:
Sembcorp Industries’ utilities unit has signed a memorandum of understanding to explore supplying renewable and low-carbon energy to Singtel’s Nxera data centres in Singapore.

They will assess power generation using low-carbon hydrogen or biomethane, solar panels fitted vertically to buildings, and electricity imported from a floating solar development at Linggiu Reservoir in Johor, Malaysia.

“AI is driving a step-change in the power needs of data centres, and in a land- and resource-constrained market like Singapore, how we source that power matters. Working with Sembcorp gives us more options to power our growth sustainably and responsibly,” says Bill Chang, CEO of Nxera and Singtel’s Digital InfraCo unit.

The Johor development is planned to have about 2.2 gigawatts of peak solar capacity. In August, Sembcorp received conditional approval for a 300-megawatt import project supported by the development, which it expects to begin operating in 2029.

“With a proven track record of powering the data centre sector, Sembcorp is well-positioned to support this growth through our diversified energy portfolio. Our partnership with Nxera further affirms our shared ambition to enable the next generation of digital infrastructure while advancing the global energy transition,” says Koh Chiap Khiong, president & CEO, Gas and Related Services and CEO of Singapore of Sembcorp.

The companies exchanged the MoU at Singapore International Energy Week on Oct 26 in the presence of Dr Tan See Leng, Minister for Energy, Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry), Singapore and Datuk Amar Haji Fadillah bin Haji Yusof, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Energy Transition and Water Transformation, Malaysia.

title: RBA warns retirement wave will test Australian pension funds
article:
(Oct 26): Australia’s central bank has warned the nation’s A$4.8 trillion (US$3.4 trillion or $4.3 trillion) pension industry is facing a fresh set of challenges as millions of people enter retirement over the next decade and funds face cash outflows as people draw down their savings.

The so-called superannuation sector has become a large owner of domestic assets and has historically been a “countercyclical stabilising force”, in times of market stress such as the Covid-19 pandemic, Reserve Bank of Australia Assistant Governor Brad Jones told the AFR Super and Wealth Summit in Melbourne on Monday.

Jones said weekly net inflows of A$1 billion-A$2 billion have historically helped the sector absorb stress. He warned that cushion may become less dependable over time as more funds move into net cash-outflow positions as more people retire and draw on their savings. About 2.5 million people are expected to retire over the next decade.

“When we look at all of that, what have been some very powerful tailwinds are going to start to become headwinds and just require more astute management,” Jones said, adding he was also concerned about concentration among some of the service providers in the industry, including funds’ administration.

Jones declined to answer a question on whether the RBA is set to hike interest rates again at its meeting next week.

Executives from two of the nation’s largest super funds, Aware Super and Australian Retirement Trust, said they had prioritised their liquidity management in anticipation of more members entering retirement and potential market shocks.

See also: 42% of Singapore respondents will only start planning for retirement within five years of their planned retirement date

“Even in the way that we’re structuring our investment team, we have deliberately put in a head of liquidity looking and focusing in on a lot of these issues” that are related to both retirement savings but also market stresses, Aware Super CEO Deanne Stewart told the same panel.
